name: Language of Parts
explanation: When a passage or phrase switches to a different language than the rest of the page, that shift needs to be marked in code with a `lang` attribute on the surrounding element. This lets assistive technology switch pronunciation rules for just that piece of text. There are exceptions: proper names, technical terms, and words that have become part of the surrounding language, like "café" in English text, don't need to be marked separately.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users depend on accurate language markup to hear foreign words pronounced correctly. Without it, a screen reader keeps using the page's main language rules straight through a quoted phrase in another language. The pronunciation that comes out doesn't match the actual words. This matters even more when scripts differ a lot, like a page switching between English and Japanese, or between left-to-right and right-to-left languages. In those cases, the wrong rules can make the text completely unintelligible when read aloud.

codeExample.bad: Our team's motto is "L'union fait la force," which drives our work.
codeExample.good: Our team's motto is "L'union fait la force," which drives our work.

howToTest: Scan the page for any passage or phrase in a language different from the page's main language. Check the HTML around each one for a `lang` attribute on the containing element, like a `<span>` or `<blockquote>`. Turn on a screen reader and listen to how it pronounces the passage. If it uses the wrong language's pronunciation rules, this fails, unless the phrase falls under an exception like a proper name or a foreign word that's become common usage.

check.question: An English-language article includes a block quote entirely in German, but the quote isn't wrapped in an element with `lang="de"`. Does this pass SC 3.1.2 Language of Parts?
choices: Yes, because the surrounding article is properly marked as English
No, because the German passage needs its own language markup so it can be pronounced correctly
Yes, because block quotes are exempt from language marking
It depends only on how long the quote is
